insights.headline: She treats total information access as the only legitimate form of safety, and builds it covertly wherever she can.
insights.explanation: The mechanism repeats across four experiences with escalating stakes: reading her mother's diary for two years (E1), reading Jeremy's two years of email at 2am (E2), holding the sole RIF list for eleven weeks (E3), and keeping every one of her mother's passwords plus reading her private emails to Roseanne (E4). In each case, having the information precedes and outlasts any operational need for it — she reads Jeremy's email though "there was nothing bad in it" and it made her "calm," she keeps the RIF list secret past the point of any decision needed from her, she reads Roseanne emails beyond the stated 80% necessary. What she calls processing or duty is also a way of never being the last to know, which is the exact inverse of what happened to her at ten.

insights.headline: She treats total information access as the only legitimate form of safety, and builds it covertly wherever she can.
insights.explanation: The mechanism repeats across four experiences with escalating stakes: reading her mother's diary for two years (E1), reading Jeremy's two years of email at 2am (E2), holding the sole RIF list for eleven weeks (E3), and keeping every one of her mother's passwords plus reading her private emails to Roseanne (E4). What she calls processing or duty is also a way of never being the last to know, which is the exact inverse of what happened to her at ten.
insights.narrator_frame: She frames each instance separately as trauma-driven ("hypervigilance," "I get very uncomfortable when I don't know where people are, mentally," "somebody has to hold the whole picture") but never names the throughline as one mechanism she deploys on purpose, repeatedly, across totally different relationships.
insights.form_evidence: Precision spikes exactly at the moment of covert access in every instance — the ribbon and page thickness (E1), the 2am floor read (E2), the exact date and page count "eleven weeks... December twentieth" (E3), the PIN composition (E4) — while the stated justification is comparatively vague ("somebody has to know," "I get uncomfortable"). The gap between forensic specificity about the access and vague abstraction about the reason is itself evidence the access is the point.

E5 does not fit this pattern directly, which is a real limit on the claim's reach but not fatal since it holds across the other four.
insights.counterexample: In E5 she leaves the group chat instead of gathering more information about her cohort — an act of information refusal, not acquisition. insights.headline: She reads exactly what a person needs before they ask, and can produce it on demand — a skill she deploys as protection more than as generosity.
insights.explanation: Across E1 (starting dinner the day the lawyer calls, being 'funny that week' when her mother is spiraling), E3 (steering Danielle away from the house purchase without ever revealing why), and E5 (noticing Tomas 'shifted' and naming it, holding R's disclosure without flinching), she demonstrates unusual, effortless attunement to what others are about to need. Others explicitly name this as her gift ("you just know me," "Alyssa's unflappable," professor's positive feedback, "that's the work"). But in each case the same skill is aimed at controlling an outcome or protecting someone from information she alone holds, not simply at connecting with them — the genius and the concealment are the same motion.
insights.narrator_frame: She names this only as compulsive over-functioning ("I take care of it before anybody has to ask... that's my whole thing") and separately as clinical competence ("that's the work... you can hold it and not flinch"), but does not connect the two as one skill serving two purposes at once.
insights.form_evidence: The moments of attunement are rendered with unusual narrative confidence and specificity (exact wording of advice to Danielle, exact clinical language to Tomas) compared to her flatter, hedged descriptions of her own needs elsewhere in the same transcripts.
insights.check: E1: L44-47 anticipatory caretaking. E3: L20-24 steering Danielle. E5: L10-11 noticing Tomas, L38-43 holding R's disclosure. E2 and E4 show the same radar turned toward monitoring (reading Jeremy's email, her mother's Roseanne correspondence) rather than toward warm anticipation, which is a variant of the same underlying attunement skill.
insights.counterexample: In E4 the radar seems to fail with Kelsey — she doesn't anticipate that Kelsey needs to be asked directly for help, and is blindsided by Kelsey's rebuttal. This suggests the genius is selective: it operates on strangers/clients/her mother but not on people she has cast as safely distant, which sharpens rather than defeats the claim.

he told me in session six that he'd never told anybody the thing he told me. And I felt — I mean, I know what the ethical answer is here, but I felt this like, click.

insights.falsifier: If she described a close relationship where she was consistently poor at anticipating needs and this was not explained by intentional distance, this claim would weaken.
insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Leadership and collaboration — as a new therapist or manager, she will be unusually accurate at predicting when a client or report is about to quit, relapse, or disclose something significant, often before any colleague notices, and will act on that read without naming it aloud until asked.

insights.headline: She protects other people's ignorance as an act of care, even when it costs her the relief of being known.
insights.explanation: She has never told Kelsey she read their mother's diary (E1, 24+ years), never told Danielle or the RIF group that she knew (E3, permanent), gave money to Terrence anonymously and insists "it was important that it was from nobody" (E3), and hasn't told Nic about her abandonment activation over the house because "I don't want to put that on him" (E5). Across decades and different people, she consistently chooses to carry a costly truth alone rather than let someone else carry the weight of knowing it, even when the disclosure would cost her little and the silence visibly costs her (weird moments at red lights, thinking about it decades later).
insights.narrator_frame: She frames the RIF-era silence as professional necessity and the Terrence gift as simple humility ("I just — it was important that it was anonymous"), not naming these as instances of one general value: that being unknown is safer for the other person than the truth.
insights.form_evidence: She volunteers each of these disclosures herself, unprompted, with a disclaimer minimizing them ("this is a weird thing to admit," "I don't even know why I'm telling you") — the compulsion to confess paired with lifelong silence toward the actual person involved is itself the tension the value sits in.
insights.check: E1: L50-52 never told Kelsey. E3: L61-66 anonymous GoFundMe gift, never disclosed. E5: L56-57 hasn't told Nic about her activation over the house.
insights.counterexample: In E5 she is fully transparent with Denise in the moment ("that lands... I have a pretty deeply grooved pattern") — but this disclosure is itself clinically fluent and performed for the room's approval, then followed by her leaving the group chat, so the deeper truth (that she felt "handled" and it cost her) stays hidden even as the performed insight is shared.

insights.falsifier: If she described telling someone the costly truth specifically to relieve her own burden, and experienced that as a relief rather than a risk, this value claim would weaken.
insights.would_predict: Relationships: Friendships and community — she will have at least one long-standing friendship where she is carrying knowledge (a past mistake, a hard feeling about the friend) that she has decided, unilaterally, the friend doesn't need or deserve to hear, and will describe protecting them as a form of loyalty.

insights.headline: In romantic and peer/professional-standing contexts, she exits at the exact moment the relationship or role becomes durable, and calls it clarity.
insights.explanation: She left Jeremy three weeks before signing a lease, the literal threshold of permanence (E2). She left the HR field four months after finally getting the senior title she'd wanted (E3). She left the cohort group chat within days of the single most bonding, vulnerable moment of the semester (E5). In E5 she names the mechanism directly for Jeremy and the house ("anytime something becomes permanent my nervous system reads permanent as, this is the thing that's going to be taken from you") but does not extend it to the job exit or the group-chat exit, both of which follow the identical shape: intimacy/commitment deepens, then she manufactures an exit dressed as principle.
insights.narrator_frame: She names this only for the romantic pattern ("I leave before I'm left... textbook") and treats the career departure and group-chat departure as separate, well-reasoned decisions (integrity, notification overload), not as instances of the same reflex.
insights.form_evidence: In both the Jeremy breakup and the group-chat exit, she delivers an articulate, closing-argument-style justification immediately after the triggering intimacy ("I gave him this whole articulate speech," "that's my attachment stuff... thank you for reflecting that") — fluent self-analysis arriving suspiciously fast, functioning to close the subject rather than open it.
insights.check: E2: L13, L36-41 leaves three weeks before lease signs. E3: L57-59 leaves job four months after promotion, right as title 'went kind of flat.' E5: L25-30 leaves group chat days after the most vulnerable exchange of the semester. E1 and E4 don't show a clean exit-at-intimacy moment — she stays in the caretaking role rather than leaving, which is a genuine limit on how far this generalizes and is reflected in the narrowed headline.
insights.counterexample: In E4 she does the opposite — she stays and over-functions rather than leaving, even when Nic offers an exit ramp (help with appointments). This suggests the mechanism is specific to peer/romantic and professional-standing contexts, not to caretaking roles where she is depended upon, which narrows rather than breaks the claim.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Career direction — in her therapy practice, once she has a caseload of long-term clients or a stable professional identity/title, she will begin to feel restless or start exploring a new specialty, role, or program within roughly a year of achieving that stability.

insights.headline: She chooses being unflappable over being comforted, even when comfort is being offered directly, because reliability is the currency she trusts more than reassurance.
insights.explanation: During the RIF (E3) she never tells anyone at the company she's struggling despite months of visible strain (shingles, closet-reorganizing at 2am) and is praised specifically for being "unflappable" — a value she protects even at direct physical cost. This is not simply over-functioning as a compulsion; it is a choice she makes even when the cost is named in her own body, suggesting reliability-as-identity is something she actively guards, not merely defaults to.
insights.narrator_frame: She names this only as a symptom to fix ("boundaries. That's my work. Saying I need something out loud") rather than as a value she is protecting on purpose — she does not say what she gets from being the unflappable one, only that she should stop.
insights.form_evidence: The physical cost (shingles at twenty-nine) is stated flatly and briefly ("I got shingles at twenty-nine. Twenty-nine!") with the repetition functioning as the only emotional emphasis, while the social reward ("you're so steady, Alyssa's unflappable") is quoted with more texture — suggesting the reward register is more real to her than the cost register.
insights.counterexample: In E5 with Denise, she does eventually say something that reads as more raw admission than performance of steadiness ("I feel like I'm being handled") — but this is reported to us, not to Denise, so it doesn't contradict the pattern of what she actually says out loud to others in real time.

insights.falsifier: If she described a workplace instance where she disclosed struggle to a colleague or supervisor before reaching a breaking point, this value claim would weaken.
insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Leadership and collaboration — as a new therapist under supervision, she will underreport her own countertransference or distress about difficult cases in supervision relative to what her supervisor would estimate from her caseload and outside observation.

insights.headline: She believes rest or care has to be earned through visible bodily breakdown, not claimed by simply asking for it.
insights.explanation: Visible across four experiences: shingles at twenty-nine (E3) forces the eventual job exit, arriving months after the strain began, not immediately; sleeping four hours and compulsive grout-cleaning (E5) is how she registers house-buying stress rather than a stated request for space; nightly swimming for a year and a half (E4) is the outlet during her mother's decline rather than delegating or asking Kelsey directly sooner; midnight kitchen rituals as a child (E1) are the only channel for an unspoken need to be seen and rewarded. In each case, physical/somatic breakdown or ritual substitutes for a direct verbal claim on rest, until the body's demand becomes loud enough to force a change.
insights.narrator_frame: She names each somatic event separately and gives it a wellness gloss ("exercise is great for the nervous system, obviously, that's well documented") rather than naming the deeper rule: that she waits for her body to force the issue rather than asking upfront.
insights.form_evidence: The physical toll is always stated with clinical distance or a joke ("I got shingles at twenty-nine. Twenty-nine!") immediately followed by a return to competence-narrative, rather than being allowed to stand as reason enough on its own to change course — the body's evidence needs a second, external trigger (the promotion going flat, Kelsey's heart emoji) before she acts.
insights.check: E1: L54-58 midnight rituals as only outlet for unspoken need. E3: L28-30 shingles as the body's protest, followed by job exit four months later, not immediately. E4: L50-54 year-and-a-half of swimming instead of asking for direct help sooner. E5: L47-48 sleep loss and compulsive cleaning during house search, addressed only via her own private therapy, not a direct request yet.
insights.counterexample: The explosive call to Kelsey (E4) is arguably a direct verbal claim, not a somatic one — but it arrives only after two years of the somatic/ritual channel was exhausted, and is triggered by anger rather than a calm stated need, which is consistent with the claim that direct requests only surface after the body/backlog route has been tried first.

insights.falsifier: If she described asking directly for rest or reduced load at the first sign of strain, before any somatic symptom or ritual appeared, this claim would weaken.
insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: Physical health — in the year following a major life transition (licensure, home purchase), she will develop a physical symptom (illness, injury, sleep disruption) that precedes any explicit conversation with Nic or a supervisor about needing to slow down.
